sources.news_title: Pentagon’s Kirsten Davies to lead White House cyber office
sources.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump named Kirsten Davies, chief information officer at the Pentagon, to lead the White House Office of the National Cyber Director, the White House said on Friday.
“Davies will drive an America First cyber strategy that treats cybersecurity as national security and keeps the United States dominant and secure in cyberspace,” the White House stated.
Davies is an advisory board member of Team8, an Israeli venture capital firm based in Tel Aviv. Before entering public service, she served as the chief information security officer at Unilever and at Estée Lauder, and founded the Institute for Cyber, a nonprofit focused on online safety and security.
Davies was sworn in as the Pentagon’s chief information officer in December 2025 after the Senate confirmed her. She advised U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth on technology and cybersecurity and oversaw efforts to modernize the military’s computer systems.
Hegseth called Davies a “dedicated patriot and professional.”
“We are confident she will advance President Trump’s America First agenda across the cybersecurity landscape,” he said.
“Our nation stands in the crossroad of analog, digital and quantum technologies, our American way of living increasingly interconnected,” Davies stated, after she was named to the new post. “Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come.”
“But only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future,” she said. “Under President Trump’s leadership, we will have a more secure, resilient and supercharged technological future.”

sources.news_title: Donald Trump’s top cybersecurity official exits amid nationwide outages after reported Stephen Miller push
sources.text:
National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross is leaving the White House, with two White House officials saying Chief of Staff Stephen Miller pushed for his removal. One official said that Cairncross “lacked the strong cyber credentials to perform the job.” Two other sources described the departure as amicable.
A person close to the White House offered a different account in an anonymous statement to a wire service, saying Cairncross was “fired” and that “the president fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position.”
Stephen Miller’s reported role in the removal
Donald Trump announced that Miller, then deputy chief of staff, would become chief of staff on November 9. In a Truth Social post, Trump called Miller “one of my most trusted advisors.”
Miller replaced Susie Wiles, who moved to the Trump political operation. Wiles wrote on X that it was her last day as chief of staff.
The change came days after Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections. Miller is best known as an architect of the administration’s immigration enforcement policies.
Kirsten Davies named to succeed Sean Cairncross
The White House named Kirsten A. Davies, the Pentagon’s chief information officer, as acting national cyber director. Davies advises Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on information management, information technology and cybersecurity. A permanent appointment to the post requires separate Senate confirmation.
Davies wrote on X that “our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come,” provided the country modernizes and builds resilience into its foundations.
Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio congratulated Davies in posts on X.
An administration official said that “Kirsten has the credentials to excel in this position and has already been Senate-confirmed.”
Davies was nominated for the Pentagon position in May 2025. The Senate confirmed her on December 18, 2025, by a 53-43 vote as part of a group of nominees. She was sworn in on December 23, 2025.
Before joining the Pentagon, Davies held senior security roles at Unilever, The Estée Lauder Companies, Barclays Africa Group, Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Siemens. She served as chief information security officer at Unilever and Estée Lauder.
A series of outages preceded the leadership change
Cairncross’ departure follows a series of technology failures across the country. A global Microsoft 365 outage began on November 12, disrupting Outlook, Teams and Copilot for nearly 24 hours. Microsoft attributed the disruption to a software defect, increased traffic and reduced server capacity.
The Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop. Officials said a newly installed Juniper router at an FAA facility in Arkansas flooded the network with data and overwhelmed an older system. The ground stop led to nearly 20,000 flight cancellations and was the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years.
The FAA later paused its router installations. JPMorgan Chase customers also experienced problems completing transactions on November 16.
Donald Trump tells Americans to ‘relax’
Trump addressed the outages in an interview with correspondent Jacqui Heinrich in Shenzhen, China, ahead of the APEC summit. Heinrich asked about growing public anxiety, including reports of Americans stockpiling food and water.
“Tell them to relax. Everything’s good,” Trump replied, describing the outages as “individual events.” He also said the press was “having a lot of fun with it.”
In the same interview, Trump addressed Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s call for billions of dollars in air traffic control funding. He said the money should not be spent “until we can do the whole thing, the whole system.”

White House taps Kirsten Davies as cyber chief after outages rattle Americans
WASHINGTON (AP) — The White House named a new national cyber director Thursday after a series of widespread service outages disrupted life and unnerved many Americans.
Kirsten Davies, chief information officer at the Defense Department, will fill the role, according to social media posts by several members of Trump’s cabinet. She will replace Sean Cairncross as the administration’s top cybersecurity official.
“Our nation stands in the crossroad of analog, digital, and quantum technologies, our American way of living increasingly interconnected,” Davies wrote in a post on X. “Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come … but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future.”
President Donald Trump faced a groundswell of criticism as Americans grappled with a cascade of service outages that snarled travel, cut off work, limited bank access and disrupted classified communications.” alt=”” />
Even staunch Trump allies accused the administration of lying to Americans or hiding information about the true cause of the disruptions. Over the past week, Microsoft, Chase Bank, air traffic control and the National Security Agency have all been affected.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday sought to assure Americans that there’s “zero” information that the technical failures are related to each other or to a malign actor.
The White House made the change as Trump returned from a three-day trip to Asia, where he downplayed the episodes, declaring that “things like that happen.”
“She has proven herself to be a dedicated patriot and professional, and we are confident she will advance President Trump’s America First agenda across the cybersecurity landscape,” Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth wrote in a post on X congratulating Davies.

sources.news_title: U.S. cyber chief resigns after a week of major technology outages as officials investigate possible links to AI-driven security patching
sources.text:
The Briefing
- Sean Cairncross, the U.S. National Cyber Director, announced his resignation on Thursday after roughly 15 months in the role; Secretary of State Marco Rubio simultaneously named cybersecurity executive Kirsten Davies as his successor.
- His departure follows a six-day stretch of technology failures — including a Microsoft 365 collapse spanning 74 countries and the longest FAA nationwide ground stop since the September 11 attacks — that struck both federal agencies and major corporations.
- A theory gaining ground in Washington, sourced to private conversations among Wall Street executives, NSA officials, and lawmakers, holds that AI-accelerated security patching — not a foreign adversary — may have set off the chain of outages.
The country's top cybersecurity official is leaving. The White House replaced National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross on Thursday, naming Kirsten Davies as his successor, departing after roughly 15 months at the helm of the Office of the National Cyber Director. Secretary of State Marco Rubio broke the news from Manila via a post on X, simultaneously naming cybersecurity and technology executive Kirsten Davies as Cairncross's replacement. 
A Political Operative in a Technical Role
Cairncross arrived in the job as a polarizing choice. The Trump administration picked him despite his having no formal cybersecurity background — his career had been built running operations at the Republican National Committee. The Senate confirmed him on August 2, 2025, in a 59-35 vote, over the objections of legislators who questioned whether a political operative could effectively guard the nation's digital infrastructure at a moment of compounding threats.
Once installed, Cairncross moved to advance the administration's cybersecurity priorities. As recently as April, he said the president was preparing to sign additional executive orders on the subject "relatively soon" — a signal that the office's agenda was still accelerating when his exit was announced.
Six Days That Shook the System
The backdrop to his resignation is a punishing run of technical failures that played out between November 12 and 17 across interconnected public and private systems. The chain began on November 12, when Microsoft's cloud services collapsed globally, leaving Outlook, Teams, and Copilot inaccessible for users in 74 countries and territories. At peak volume, outage-tracking sites logged nearly 130,000 user complaints for Outlook alone in the United States. Recovery stretched into a second day before services were fully restored.
The next day brought a new front. On Friday, November 13, the Federal Aviation Administration declared a nationwide aviation shutdown, grounding all departing flights and citing intermittent communication failures across multiple air traffic control centers. The nationwide ground stop lasted from about 3:30 p.m. to 8:15 p.m. ET. Airlines cancelled approximately 12,462 flights on November 13. It was only the second time the FAA had halted departures across the entire country since September 11, 2001.
Banks, Intelligence Agencies, and Apple Also Hit
The disruptions spread further. A software defect in JPMorgan Chase's on-premise hardware slowed transactions at the country's largest bank, while users at Bank of America, U.S. Bank, and Wells Fargo reported service interruptions that included Zelle payment failures tracked by monitoring platforms.
Then, on November 17, the intelligence community was pulled into the crisis. The NSA attributed the temporary network disruption to scheduled routine maintenance, a flaw that could allow attackers to gain remote control of servers. That same day, an internal Apple update triggered disruptions to Apple Pay and iCloud.
Washington Rules Out a Coordinated Attack
Senior officials moved quickly to tamp down speculation that a foreign power or criminal network had orchestrated the cascade. Speaking from Manila, Rubio maintained the incidents were unrelated and that investigators had found no evidence pointing to hackers, criminal organizations, or adversarial governments. He drew distinct lines between each failure, arguing each had a separate and independent cause. President Trump also weighed in publicly, downplaying the severity and assuring the public the situation would be "completely under control."
Officials and companies attributed several high-profile disruptions to technical problems and said they had found no evidence that the incidents were connected or caused by a cyberattack.
The AI Patching Theory: When the Cure Triggers the Crisis
Beneath the official reassurances, a more unsettling explanation has circulated in Washington. The Washington Sun, drawing on sources familiar with private exchanges between Wall Street executives, NSA officials, and congressional members, reported that A report by The Washington Sun, citing sources familiar with private discussions, said efforts to patch vulnerabilities identified by AI models may have contributed to some of the outages. Under that reading, the very tools deployed to reinforce digital defenses inadvertently destabilized interconnected infrastructure by pushing updates too aggressively.
If that account holds, the week's failures would be reframed not as a story of outside threats but as a failure of internal risk management — and would call into question how much automation the U.S. government and its corporate partners can safely apply to their most sensitive systems.
A New Director Steps Into the Fire
The House Homeland Security Committee had already held a hearing on the incidents by the time Davies's appointment was announced. She inherits an office whose mandate — coordinating federal cybersecurity strategy across dozens of agencies and sustaining partnerships with the private sector — has rarely felt more urgent. The central question now facing Washington is whether a change of leadership at the top of the nation's cyber apparatus is sufficient, or whether a broader structural reckoning lies ahead.

sources.news_title: Trump Fires White House Cybersecurity Director Amid Nationwide Technology Outages, Names Pentagon Official as Replacement
sources.text:
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
President Donald Trump’s administration removed White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross on Thursday, Nov. 19, following a series of major technology outages affecting airlines, financial institutions and national security systems, as administration officials raised concerns about his qualifications to oversee federal cybersecurity policy.
Cairncross, who had served as the administration’s top cybersecurity adviser since August 2025, was dismissed with Trump’s support, according to officials familiar with the decision. Kirsten Davies, the Pentagon’s chief information officer, was selected to replace him and assume responsibility for coordinating cybersecurity strategy across the federal government.
A source close to the White House told ABC News that Trump believed Cairncross “lacked the strong cyber credentials to perform the job.” The personnel change followed several days of widespread disruptions, although authorities have not established that the outages were caused by cyberattacks or failures directly attributable to Cairncross.
The decision was also influenced by White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, who had expressed concerns about Cairncross’ qualifications and supported replacing him, according to reporting by CBS News.
Cairncross’ departure came as federal officials investigated an unusual concentration of technology failures affecting critical services nationwide.
Among the most disruptive incidents was a Federal Aviation Administration communications failure that prompted a nationwide ground stop Nov. 13, interrupting more than 18,000 flights. Investigators subsequently linked the problem to a contractor’s work involving copper wiring at an Arkansas radio facility.
Additional failures affected Microsoft services, major banking institutions and computer networks used by the National Security Agency.
The NSA experienced an internal communications outage Tuesday during routine maintenance, raising concerns about the resilience of technology supporting classified government operations.
Federal officials have cautioned against interpreting the disruptions as evidence of a coordinated attack.
During congressional testimony Wednesday, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said investigators had not identified evidence connecting the incidents to a single malicious operation.
“Based on what we know today, after a great deal of diligence, these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack,” Clayton said.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin similarly told lawmakers that investigators had found no evidence establishing a connection among the outages. He expressed strong confidence that the incidents did not result from hostile foreign cyber activity, although he acknowledged the unusual concentration of disruptions.
The administration’s cybersecurity leadership change was first reported by Axios, which identified Davies as Cairncross’ successor and described the decision as part of a broader effort to strengthen federal cybersecurity leadership.
Cairncross, an attorney and former Republican political operative, previously worked as chief operating officer of the Republican National Committee and held senior positions in Trump’s political and governmental operations.
Before becoming national cyber director, he had not accumulated extensive professional experience directly managing cybersecurity operations.
His appointment placed him in charge of the Office of the National Cyber Director, a White House organization established in 2021 to coordinate federal cybersecurity policies, advise the president and oversee strategic efforts to protect government systems and critical infrastructure.
The position requires Senate confirmation and carries responsibility for coordinating policy across agencies involved in national security, telecommunications, technology and federal information systems.
During his tenure, Cairncross oversaw development of the administration’s national cybersecurity strategy, released in March 2026.
The seven-page strategy outlined priorities including strengthening critical infrastructure, modernizing federal technology, maintaining American leadership in artificial intelligence and confronting foreign adversaries attempting to penetrate government and private networks.
At the Aspen Cyber Summit in November 2025, Cairncross emphasized the need to impose consequences on countries and organizations conducting malicious cyber operations against the United States.
“I think, as a country, we have not done a terrific job of sending a signal to our adversaries that this behavior is not consequence-free,” Cairncross said. “And we need to do that because it is scaling and it is becoming more aggressive every passing day.”
In a statement following his departure, Cairncross described his service as national cyber director as “the honor of a lifetime.”
“I leave my role as Director of Cyber incredibly proud of our work to strengthen America’s cybersecurity, protect our critical infrastructure, confront foreign threats, and position America to lead the world in Super Intelligence. None of it would have been possible without President Trump’s extraordinary leadership,” he said.
Davies, his replacement, brings experience overseeing technology operations and information security in both government and private industry.
As the Defense Department’s chief information officer, she has been responsible for managing information technology strategy, cybersecurity priorities and digital modernization across one of the federal government’s largest and most complex organizations.
Her appointment comes as federal agencies face growing pressure to protect critical networks against increasingly sophisticated threats, including attacks associated with foreign intelligence services and criminal organizations.
According to reporting by Nextgov/FCW, the leadership change creates additional uncertainty within an administration already confronting cybersecurity staffing challenges and disputes over agency resources.
The administration has made changes to federal cybersecurity personnel and organizational structures during Trump’s second term, including leadership changes at the National Security Agency and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.
Those developments have generated congressional scrutiny over whether federal cybersecurity organizations possess sufficient staffing, technical expertise and resources to respond to emerging threats.
During a Senate confirmation hearing Thursday, Michael LoSapio, Trump’s nominee to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, faced questions about the government’s readiness to withstand major cyberattacks.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., pressed LoSapio about whether the agency would need to replace employees dismissed during earlier federal workforce reductions.
“I’m going to investigate and dig in and understand where our gaps are and, if needed, come back to this committee and request more resources,” LoSapio said.
The discussion highlighted broader concerns about federal cybersecurity capabilities as government agencies confront technology disruptions and increasingly complex digital security threats.
Davies will assume leadership of the White House cybersecurity office as officials continue investigating the recent outages and evaluating safeguards for essential government networks.
Although Cairncross’ removal followed the widespread service failures, investigators have not established that the disruptions resulted from a coordinated cyberattack, and the administration has not publicly demonstrated that his leadership contributed directly to the incidents.
The appointment of Davies marks a significant personnel change in the Trump administration’s cybersecurity operations, placing a Pentagon technology executive in charge of coordinating federal efforts to protect critical infrastructure, strengthen government networks and respond to emerging threats.

sources.news_title: After Weeks of Tech Meltdowns, Trump Dumps Cybersecurity Director
sources.text:
The face of the Trump administration's cybersecurity policy has left the team. White House National Cybersecurity Director Sean Cairncross is out, to be replaced by Department of Defense Chief Information Officer Kirsten A. Davies.
Axios reported Cairncross's departure on Thursday, citing two unnamed White House officials who said Chief of Staff Stephen Miller wanted him gone for lacking "strong cyber credentials to perform the job."
During a White House press briefing on Friday, Trump said he dumped Cairncross because, "I didn't think that person was good enough."
That wasn't a problem when the administration nominated Cairncross in February 2025. The White House statement applauding the executive's confirmation by the Senate last August cited his "extensive leadership experience" as CEO of the Millennium Challenge Corporation, a federal foreign-development agency, and as a senior advisor in Trump's first White House.
Cairncross then became the administration's most visible figure in introducing policy shifts, such as the brief cybersecurity strategy document published in May and its emphasis on imposing unspecified consequences on adversaries for hostile actions.
At Black Hat in August, Cairncross used his conference-opening keynote to tell information-security companies that the Trump administration would stay out of their way. "We want to make sure that we are working hand in glove and collaboratively with industry," he said, adding that any "regulatory regime" would "strangle growth, development, and innovation and be enormously harmful to the industry."
The last two weeks of tech breakdowns at Microsoft, Apple, and big-name banks have not exactly burnished the tech industry's image, even though these breakdowns don't appear to be the result of any hacking attempts. Instead, the issue behind many of them seems to be a rush to patch vulnerabilities uncovered by AI tools.
Davies, announced Friday by the White House as Cairncross's acting replacement pending Senate confirmation, has a much stronger background in information security. Her biography on the Pentagon's website notes her prior work as Unilever's chief information security officer as well as earlier "technology and cyber roles" at Estée Lauder Companies, Barclays, Hewlett Packard Enterprises, and Siemens.
The national cyber director has had such a prominent role in Trump 2.0 in part because the White House has marginalized the Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the office established under Trump 1.0 to lead government infosec efforts.
DOGE-driven layoffs reduced CISA's staff by about a third (although subsequent hiring efforts have replenished some of the agency's staff); President Trump has attempted to derail the careers of previous CISA directors Chris Krebs and Jen Easterly for upholding the integrity of the 2020 election, and the White House has yet to nominate somebody to head CISA that the Senate can accept.
The latest such pick, former Palantir CISO Michael LoSapio, seems doomed after a disastrous confirmation hearing on Thursday. As Cybersecurity Dive's Eric Geller related in a recap, LoSapio dodged such basic questions as whether those layoffs hurt the agency ("I can't comment on the current state of CISA, because I'm not inside today") and what the Jan. 6, 2021, insurrection at the Capitol represented ("I don't believe it was an attack").
Sens. Thom Tillis (R-NC) and Ron Wyden (D-OR) then placed holds on LoSapio's nomination, with Wyden telling NextGov/FCW: "You can't have an insurrectionist Palantir executive in charge of our nation's cybersecurity and election security."

sources.news_title: Pentagon CIO replaces White House national cyber director after tech outages
sources.text:
White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross was fired from his job, a person close to the White House said on Thursday, days after technology outages disrupted U.S. air travel, banking and national security systems.
Department of Defense Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies will assume the position temporarily, according to the source. Davies confirmed the appointment in a post on X, in which she thanked President Donald Trump, White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
“Under President Trump’s leadership we will have a more secure, resilient; and supercharged technological future,” Davies wrote.
Davies was sworn in as the Pentagon’s CIO in December 2025 and was responsible for the department’s digital infrastructure. She previously served as chief information security officer for Unilever and held technology and cyber roles at The Estée Lauder Companies, Barclays-Africa Group, Hewlett Packard Enterprises and Siemens, according to her Pentagon biography.
Cairncross’s ouster comes as Trump and his administration face mounting scrutiny over their response to the series of disruptions over the past week, including a global outage affecting hundreds of millions of Microsoft users and a nationwide halt to air travel that disrupted more than 18,000 flights. Next week will test the nation’s technology systems, as millions of travelers take to the skies to visit loved ones for Thanksgiving and retailers prepare for a surge of Black Friday online shopping.
The dismissal of Cairncross is the administration’s first major personnel move since the outages began.
Cairncross oversaw cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal government.
“The president fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position,” said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Cairncross said in a statement on Thursday night it was the “honor of a lifetime to serve” in Trump’s administration.
The recent technology disruptions are likely linked to corporate efforts to rapidly patch newly discovered software vulnerabilities in the AI age, cybersecurity experts told Reuters. Advanced AI tools make it easier for companies to uncover weaknesses in their cybersecurity protections.
The top U.S. intelligence official said on Wednesday the disruptions were separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes and not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.
Republican Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri on Tuesday told reporters in Washington the Trump administration should brief lawmakers on the outages so they can “share with the American people what’s happening here.”
Cairncross was an executive at the Republican National Committee before assuming the cyber director role. Congress established the position shortly before former President Joe Biden took office. Previous cyber directors had technology and national security experience.
His successor will need to be confirmed by the Senate, which will be controlled by Democrats beginning in January.

Trump Fires His Cyber Guy After Widespread Tech Outages
“I didn’t think he was good enough.”
Sean Cairncross
Mandel Ngan/AFP/Getty Images
Sean Cairncross
President Donald Trump’s top cybersecurity official is leaving his role at a pretty inopportune time.
National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross is stepping down as the White House scrambles to deal with the recent wave of outages and cyber threats, according to The Wall Street Journal. He’ll be replaced by Kirsten Davis, the chief information officer at the Defense Department.
When asked Friday why he fired Cairncross, President Donald Trump answered, “because I didn’t think he was good enough.”
Q: Why did you fire the cyber chief yesterday?
TRUMP: Because I didn't think that person was good enough https://t.co/pFHKS1Lf4m
Cairncross was the face of the administration’s artificial intelligence strategy—which, if his replacement is any indication, is clearly not going too well. He was part of the first Trump White House, and is a longtime official at the Republican National Committee. He did not have any cyber experience when he was made national cyber director.
Many of the outages across the country have been attributed to issues with code upgrades, hastily patched through in order to try to protect from the emerging vulnerabilities caused by AI. The Trump administration has been struggling to respond to the cyber issues, and instead has been putting oblivious officials like Markwayne Mullin on TV to speculate. And the Federal Aviation Administration is still only “very close” to figuring out why planes had to be grounded nationwide last week.
Trump Snipes at Elon Musk After He Says He’s “Not MAGA”
It looks like Donald Trump and Musk are headed for another messy breakup.
Donald Trump and Elon Musk
Tierney L. Cross/The Washington Post/Bloomberg/Getty Images
Donald Trump and Elon Musk
America’s billionaire president is picking a fight with the world’s richest man.
Donald Trump issued a thinly veiled threat against Elon Musk Thursday, telling NBC News that when people “veer” away from his MAGA movement, “they don’t do very well.”
The remark came hours after Musk—who spent nearly half a billion dollars on the Republican Party’s midterm bust—unequivocally declared that he’s “not MAGA” at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit.
“If that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that,” Musk said at the time.
Musk did the interview from China, where he was part of Trump’s delegation at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
“I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it,” Musk said in another part of the DealBook exchange, reacting to his midterm expenses. “But it certainly shows that, you know, American elections are not just about money.”
The trillionaire said that he spent so much money on Republican candidates and conservative groups because “it’s good to have some balance of power.” Despite the fact that Republicans controlled the White House and Congress at the time of the election, Musk noted that “as a general rule” he wouldn’t want “the presidency, Senate, and House all to be of the same party.”
“Probably, if I could rewind the clock,” he said, “I would have spent less money.”
The comments mark a stark ideological divorce for Musk, who spent most of last year effectively dismantling the federal government after Trump granted him special government employee status. At one point, it appeared that Musk’s influence over Trump was so extreme that the general public began to speculate about whether it was Trump or Musk running the country.
“He’s a friend of mine,” Trump told NBC News on Thursday, responding to Musk’s rebuke. “What can I tell you? I mean, you have to ask—there are lots of definitions out there. MAGA, to me, means something very specific, and when people veer from it, they don’t do very well.”
“But Elon is—Elon’s got very good intentions,” the president continued. “I mean, he was with me the whole—he traveled with me.”
Dozens of Staffers Leave Bari Weiss’s CBS in “Extinction-Level Event”
Staffers from across the company took buyouts.
CBS News chief Bari Weiss
David Paul Morris/Bloomberg/Getty Images
CBS News chief Bari Weiss
A wave of buyouts at CBS News has resulted in dozens of departures from every corner of the company.
CBS News staff were given until Wednesday to accept a buyout from Skydance, the company owned by David Ellison, the son of Trump’s good friend Larry Ellison.
One CBS News staffer told Status the departures were an “extinction-level event.” The buyouts have reportedly decimated the foreign news desk: Puck News’s Dylan Byers reported that one-third of the organization’s London office took buyouts. The buyouts also saw departures from 60 Minutes, the Evening News, and the network’s bureau in Washington.
Mounting reports suggest that CBS News’s foreign coverage has struggled under the leadership of Bari Weiss, who has repeatedly placed her own pro-Israel politics at the center of the organization’s reporting. Last month, Weiss reportedly became “very, very hands-on” with a story about violent Israeli settlers driving Palestinians out of the West Bank. By: Neil Lomack
President Donald Trump’s administration is undergoing a significant cybersecurity leadership shake-up following the departure of National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross, whose removal comes amid an extraordinary succession of technological disruptions affecting American aviation, banking institutions, communications networks and sensitive national security systems.
The New York Times reported Thursday that Cairncross, the White House’s highest-ranking cybersecurity coordinator, was leaving the administration after approximately 15 months in office. His departure coincides with mounting public anxiety over the reliability of America’s increasingly interconnected technological infrastructure.
Although federal officials insist that the recent outages were unrelated to malicious cyberattacks, the unprecedented concentration of disruptions has intensified scrutiny of the government’s ability to anticipate, investigate and manage potentially catastrophic technological failures.
According to a Reuters report, a person close to the White House subsequently confirmed that Cairncross had been dismissed. “The president fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position,” the source told Reuters.
The administration is expected to appoint Kirsten Davies, currently the Defense Department’s chief information officer, as acting national cyber director.
The New York Times reported that the country has experienced a remarkable succession of technology failures, disrupting routine commercial activities and critical government operations.
Problems affecting Microsoft services interfered with electronic communications, while technical disruptions at major financial institutions complicated banking transactions.
A nationwide aviation shutdown temporarily halted commercial flights, creating extensive travel delays and raising concerns about the resilience of air traffic control infrastructure.
Perhaps most troubling was a temporary outage affecting an internal communications network at the National Security Agency, one of America’s principal intelligence organizations.
The New York Times described the sequence of failures as contributing to a growing perception that essential national systems were becoming dangerously vulnerable.
Despite public speculation about coordinated cyberwarfare, senior administration officials have repeatedly rejected suggestions that the incidents originated from a common hostile operation.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told lawmakers that investigators had “seen nothing that would indicate that they are related.”
According to CBS News, Mullin expressed 98 percent confidence that the disruptions were not attributable to malicious foreign activity. Nevertheless, he acknowledged that he had not previously encountered so many major outages within such a compressed period.
The distinction between a cyberattack and an ordinary technological malfunction remains crucial. A system failure can produce enormous economic disruption without involving hackers, foreign intelligence services or deliberate sabotage.

The New York Times has separately examined how failures affecting individual technological components can cascade across industries, producing consequences far beyond their immediate origins.
Experts warn that the increasing integration of artificial intelligence into critical systems could introduce additional vulnerabilities, even as emerging technologies provide sophisticated tools for identifying and correcting software defects.

Axios initially reported that his departure was amicable and reflected his reluctance to remain in the position for another two years. As The New York Times report emphasized, the public’s growing unease reflects not merely the inconvenience of isolated outages, but uncertainty about whether essential technological infrastructure can withstand increasingly sophisticated threats and unexpected failures.

Ashley’s view
Someone was bound to take the fall for a string of tech outages that have left the country terrified about what services might get disrupted next — even if the most basic (and likely true) explanation is that organizations are rushing to patch software bugs discovered by AI programs and are crashing their systems in the process.

Davies takes over the office that coordinates federal cybersecurity policy after six days of technology failures that cut off workplace email around the world, halted flights across the country, slowed payments at the nation’s largest bank and knocked out services at Apple and a classified network at the NSA.
The first came Nov. 12, when a defect in Microsoft 365 knocked Outlook offline in 74 countries and disrupted productivity tools for nearly a day. A day later, the FAA halted departures nationwide for more than four hours after L3Harris deployed a new router which destabilized 17 of 22 air route traffic control centers.
Online banking faltered after the weekend, when JPMorgan Chase said that a software bug in on-premise hardware had slowed its transactions and held up payments for customers at other banks and on Zelle. Apple followed the next day, blaming an internal update for disruptions to iCloud, the App Store and Apple Pay. That same day, the NSA’s classified internal network, known as NSANet, went down and forced staff to stagger their arrivals at Fort Meade, Maryland.
A rush to fix software flaws identified with artificial intelligence appears to be behind most of the outages, two people familiar with the matter told Nextgov/FCW.
The officials who briefed Congress, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia, testified before the House Homeland Security Committee on Nov. 18. Clayton told lawmakers that “the rate of patching, the rate of upgrading of systems is increasing,” while Mullin said he was “98 percent confident” that adversaries were not behind the failures.
Lawmakers from both parties questioned that assessment, with Rep. Nick LaLota, R-N.Y., calling the events “a little beyond coincidences” and Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., saying the White House had offered no clear explanation and that “people are freaking out.” Asked on Fox on Nov. 19 whether the public should prepare for emergencies, Trump said, “Tell them to relax, everything is good, these are individual events.”
What’s Next: A permanent national cyber director requires Senate confirmation, which will fall to a Democratic-controlled Senate starting in January. Trump’s pick to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, Palantir executive Michael LoSapio, faces holds pledged by Sens. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., and Ron Wyden, D-Ore., after his Nov. 19 confirmation hearing. The FAA has paused installation of more than 60 Juniper routers while it reevaluates when it schedules replacement work.

sources.news_title: White House Cyber Director Ousted Amid Major Tech Outages
sources.text:
White House Cyber Director Sean Cairncross is leaving the Trump administration amid heightened scrutiny of major technology outages that have disrupted government operations and private-sector services, creating another leadership change at a time when federal cybersecurity systems are under pressure.
Cairncross, who served as the national cyber director, is departing after less than two years in the position. His exit comes as federal officials investigate a series of technology disruptions, including an outage involving a highly classified National Security Agency communications network.
CBS News and Reuters reported that Cairncross was removed from his position. However, accounts of the circumstances surrounding his departure have differed, with other reporting describing the separation as voluntary or amicable.

The conflicting accounts leave questions about whether Cairncross was dismissed, resigned or reached an agreement to leave the administration.
The White House Office of the National Cyber Director is responsible for coordinating federal cybersecurity policy across government agencies. The office also works with Congress, private companies and national security officials to address cyber threats and strengthen the country’s defenses against digital attacks.
Unlike agencies that directly investigate cybercrimes or operate intelligence networks, the office focuses primarily on developing and coordinating cybersecurity strategy across the federal government.
Cairncross’s departure comes during a particularly sensitive period for that work.
Over the past week, technology failures have affected air travel, banking services, Microsoft platforms and federal national security systems. A nationwide ground stop disrupted more than 18,000 flights, while an outage involving Microsoft’s services affected users attempting to access email and other online tools.
The National Security Agency also experienced a temporary disruption to NSANet, its classified internal communications network. According to The Associated Press, the agency said the interruption occurred during scheduled maintenance and that its most critical operations remained functional through backup systems.
Despite the unusual concentration of outages, federal officials have cautioned against assuming they were connected.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told lawmakers this week that investigators had found no evidence linking the incidents. He said he was 98% confident the disruptions were not caused by malicious foreign activity.
Other senior intelligence officials have described the incidents as separate technical failures involving maintenance, software changes and system updates.
There is currently no verified evidence that the outages resulted from a coordinated cyberattack or that Cairncross personally contributed to the disruptions.
The leadership shakeup also appears connected to changes within Trump’s senior White House staff.
According to CBS News, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller had pushed for Cairncross’s removal because he questioned whether the director possessed sufficient cybersecurity expertise. Miller replaced Susie Wiles earlier this month.
Reuters separately reported that a person close to the White House said Trump supported dismissing Cairncross over concerns about his qualifications.
Cairncross is an attorney and longtime Republican political operative who previously served as chief operating officer of the Republican National Committee. During Trump’s first administration, he also held senior government positions, including leading the Millennium Challenge Corporation, a federal foreign assistance agency.
He was confirmed by the Senate in August 2025 by a vote of 59 to 35.
Although Cairncross had extensive political and government management experience, he did not have a substantial technical cybersecurity background before assuming the position.
His responsibilities included advising Trump on national cybersecurity strategy, coordinating policies across federal agencies and helping develop approaches to emerging threats involving artificial intelligence.
The White House has selected Kirsten Davies, currently the Pentagon’s chief information officer, to assume the national cyber director’s responsibilities on an acting basis.
Davies brings experience overseeing information technology and cybersecurity operations within the Defense Department, one of the federal government’s largest and most complex technology organizations.
Her appointment comes as the administration faces additional questions about cybersecurity leadership across the federal government.
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, known as CISA, is responsible for helping protect federal civilian networks and critical infrastructure, including energy systems, communications networks and election infrastructure.
The agency has been operating without a Senate-confirmed permanent director while Trump’s nominee, Michael LoSapio, moves through the confirmation process.
Cairncross’s replacement will also require Senate confirmation. That process could become more complicated after Democrats assume control of the Senate in January following the November midterm elections.
The latest disruptions have also attracted attention from lawmakers. Republican Sen. Josh Hawley has called for the administration to brief Congress on the outages and the government’s response.
The consequences of major technology failures extend beyond Washington. Americans depend on interconnected computer systems to access bank accounts, board flights, receive government services and communicate with businesses.
Even when an outage is not caused by hackers, disruptions can expose weaknesses in the systems that support everyday services.
The Office of the National Cyber Director plays a coordinating role in addressing those vulnerabilities, particularly when problems involve multiple federal agencies or industries.
For now, Davies will be responsible for helping oversee the administration’s cybersecurity strategy while federal officials continue examining the recent outages.
The White House has not announced a permanent replacement for Cairncross or established a public timeline for submitting a new nominee to the Senate.

sources.news_title: 'Fully supported firing': Donald Trump backs removal of US cyber chief Sean Cairncross
sources.text:
‘Fully supported firing’: Donald Trump backs removal of US cyber chief Sean Cairncross
US President Donald Trump has backed the reported firing of National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross as a series of technology outages hit critical infrastructure, banks, airlines and government networks.
New Delhi: US National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross is set to leave his post as several technology disruptions have affected critical infrastructure, financial institutions and government networks across the country.
A person close to the White House told AFP on Thursday that Cairncross had been “fired” and said US President Donald Trump “fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position”. The source cited concerns over whether Cairncross had the right credentials for the role.
However, Fox News reported a different account, saying Cairncross did not want to remain in the position for another two years. It remains unclear when exactly he will leave.
According to NBC News, Kirsten Davies, the Department of Defense’s Chief Information Officer, is expected to take over as acting National Cyber Director. The position requires Senate confirmation for a permanent appointment. Davies has already been confirmed by the Senate and was described by the source as having more suitable credentials.
Who is Sean Cairncross?
Cairncross has led the Office of the National Cyber Director since August 2025. The office coordinates cybersecurity policy and strategy across the US government.
He previously held several positions in the White House during Trump’s first administration and was also the Republican National Committee’s Chief Operating Officer during the 2016 election cycle. Cairncross declined to comment on his reported departure.
His exit comes amid a string of technology disruptions in the US. These have included a nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground stop, Microsoft Outlook outages, disruptions involving United Airlines and major banks, and a temporary interruption to an internal National Security Agency communications network.
US officials dismiss cyberattack link
The incidents have raised concerns over the security of critical infrastructure. However, the country’s top intelligence official said on Wednesday that the disruptions were separate service outages caused by maintenance and technical changes, rather than a coordinated or state-backed cyberattack.
JPMorgan Chase also disclosed that third-party service providers working with the bank had been targeted in a cyberattack. The bank said some marketing data held by vendors may have been accessed including customer names, email addresses, phone numbers and account identifiers.
Trump has meanwhile played down concerns over the wider disruptions, saying, “Tell them to relax. Everything’s good. These are individual events.” The White House has not indicated how long Davies will serve in the acting role.
